passages.title: The Ice Cube Race
passages.passage:
Last month my science teacher set an unusual piece of homework. Instead of answering questions from the textbook, we had to design an experiment that could be done at home with things from the kitchen, and then write down exactly what happened. My younger brother Bao, who is nine, decided at once that he was going to help me, whether I wanted him to or not.

We chose a simple question: which material keeps an ice cube frozen for the longest time? I took six ice cubes of the same size out of the freezer and placed each one in a small bowl. One was wrapped in aluminium foil, one in a cotton sock, one in a plastic bag, one in newspaper, one in a woollen glove, and the last was left uncovered so that we had something to compare the others with. Bao wrote the starting time on a sheet of paper and set a timer to ring every ten minutes.

The results surprised both of us. I had expected the foil to win, because I thought metal would keep the cold in. In fact, the foil cube melted second fastest, just after the uncovered one. The glove was the clear winner: after fifty minutes, its ice cube was still about half its original size. Bao's explanation was that "the glove is warm, so the ice must like it". Mine was that wool traps air, and air is a poor conductor of heat, so warmth from the room could not reach the ice easily.

When I handed in the report, my teacher was less interested in which material had won than in how we had made the test fair. She pointed out that we had done one thing right without knowing it: all the bowls had sat on the same table, away from the window. Next time, she suggested, we should repeat the experiment three times before trusting the result.

Bao is already planning to test our mother's winter scarf.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: A home experiment on keeping ice frozen and what the writer learned from it
Why wool is warmer than metal in winter
A nine-year-old boy who wants to become a scientist
How a science teacher marks homework reports
questions.explanation: The passage follows one experiment from the homework task to the teacher's comments. Wool and Bao are details inside that story, not the topic of the whole text.

questions.q: Why was one ice cube left uncovered?
options: Because Bao forgot to wrap the last one
So that the wrapped cubes could be compared with it
Because the teacher asked for exactly six cubes
Because the writer ran out of materials to wrap it in
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the last cube was left uncovered so that we had something to compare the others with. Nothing suggests a mistake or a shortage of materials.

questions.q: Which material did the writer expect to keep the ice frozen longest?
options: The plastic bag
The woollen glove
The aluminium foil
The newspaper
questions.explanation: The writer says I had expected the foil to win because metal seemed likely to keep the cold in. The glove is what actually won, which is a different question.

questions.q: What can be inferred about the teacher's attitude to the experiment?
options: She was disappointed that the foil lost
She believed the experiment should not be done at home
She thought the result was probably wrong
She cared more about the method than about which material won
questions.explanation: She was less interested in which material had won than in how we had made the test fair, praised the fair placing of the bowls and asked for repeats. That is a focus on method, not on the winner.

questions.q: In paragraph 3, the word "traps" is closest in meaning to
options: holds in and stops from escaping
pushes out
catches an animal
warms up
questions.explanation: Wool traps air means it holds air inside its fibres so the air cannot move away. The sentence goes on to explain why that trapped air keeps warmth from reaching the ice.

questions.q: In paragraph 3, "Mine" refers to
options: the writer's ice cube
the writer's explanation
the writer's glove
the writer's report
questions.explanation: The previous sentence gives Bao's explanation; "Mine" is the writer's explanation, set against it.

questions.q: The ice cube wrapped in foil melted faster than the uncovered one.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The foil cube melted second fastest, just after the uncovered one, so the uncovered cube melted first and the foil cube was slower, not faster.

passages.title: Before the Town Wakes Up
passages.passage:
Most people in Phu An know the bakery on Market Street by its smell rather than its name. By half past five in the morning, long before the shutters of the other shops go up, the scent of warm bread is already drifting across the square. The sign above the door says "Hoa Bakery", but everyone simply calls it "the bakery", as if there could be no other.

Mrs Hoa opened the shop twenty-eight years ago with a single oven and a recipe for baguettes that she had learned from her aunt. In those days she baked everything herself and sold it through a window, because there was no room inside for customers. Today the bakery has three ovens, a small café with six tables, and a team of five, including her son Duc, who left a job in the city to come home and take over the early shift.

Duc has introduced some changes, not all of them popular at first. He replaced the paper bags with cloth ones that customers bring back, added a shelf of wholemeal loaves, and started posting photographs of each morning's bread online. "Some of the older customers said we were showing off," he admits. "But then their grandchildren started coming in to see whether the bread looked as good as the pictures."

The bakery's busiest hour is between six and seven, when workers from the fish market and students from the secondary school queue together on the pavement. Anything left unsold at four in the afternoon is given to the pagoda at the end of the street, which cooks for elderly people who live alone.

Mrs Hoa still arrives at four every morning, although she says she no longer needs to. "The bread would be fine without me," she says. "But I wouldn't be fine without the bread." Her son, standing behind her with flour on his sleeves, does not argue.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the passage?
options: A guide to the best places to eat in Phu An
The story of a long-established bakery and how it is changing
An argument that small shops should sell their bread online
A description of a typical morning at a fish market
questions.explanation: The text moves from the bakery's beginnings to the son's changes and the mother's continuing role. The fish market and online photos appear only as details.

questions.q: Why did Mrs Hoa originally sell bread through a window?
options: Because the shop had no space for customers
Because it kept the bread warm for longer
Because her aunt had sold bread in the same way
Because customers preferred not to come inside
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 gives the reason directly: there was no room inside for customers. The aunt is mentioned only as the source of the recipe.

questions.q: How did some older customers first react to the photographs online?
options: They brought their grandchildren to see the bread
They asked for copies of the pictures
They stopped coming to the bakery
They felt the bakery was showing off
questions.explanation: Duc admits that some of the older customers said we were showing off. The grandchildren came on their own, later, to check the bread against the pictures.

questions.q: In paragraph 1, the word "drifting" is closest in meaning to
options: being blown away by a strong wind
rising quickly
moving slowly through the air
disappearing completely
questions.explanation: The scent of bread drifting across the square spreads gently and slowly; the calm early-morning picture rules out a strong wind or a sudden rise.

questions.q: Why does the writer end the passage with Mrs Hoa's words about the bread?
options: To show that the bakery cannot run without her
To show how strongly she is attached to her work
To suggest that she and her son disagree about the future
To explain why the bakery opens so early
questions.explanation: She admits the bread would be fine without me but that she would not be fine without it, which shows attachment, not necessity. Her son's silence suggests agreement, not disagreement.

questions.q: Bread that is not sold by the afternoon is offered at a lower price.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: Paragraph 4 says unsold bread is given to the pagoda, which cooks for elderly people. It is given away, not sold more cheaply.

questions.q: Duc trained as a baker while he was in the city.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: We are told only that he left a job in the city; the passage never says what that job was or where he learned to bake.

passages.title: The Morning the Road Disappeared
passages.passage:
When I woke up, the light in my bedroom was wrong. It was too white, and too quiet. My first thought was that I had overslept and missed the bus. Then I pulled back the curtain and understood: the street, the cars, the roofs and the small park opposite had all disappeared under a thick layer of snow, and more was still falling.

We had moved to the town only in September, and my parents had warned me that winters here were serious. Even so, none of us was ready for that morning. My father spent twenty minutes searching for the car before he gave up, and my mother discovered that the front door would not open until we had pushed the snow away from the outside with a kitchen tray.

At half past seven, the message came through from school: closed for the day, all after-school activities cancelled, "stay safe and enjoy it". I read the last three words twice. In my old city, a day off school meant a storm, and a storm meant staying indoors with the windows shut. Here, apparently, it meant something else.

By nine o'clock the park was full. Children I only knew by sight from the school corridors were dragging plastic sleds up the slope and racing down it, screaming. A boy from my maths class, Tomas, handed me a spare sled without a word and pointed at the top. I fell off three times on the first run. On the fourth, I reached the bottom still sitting, and somebody cheered.

We stayed out until our gloves were soaked through. At home, my mother had made hot chocolate, and my father had finally found the car, by walking into it. The next morning the roads were cleared and the bus came as usual. But in the corridor, Tomas nodded at me, and it felt as if the town had opened a door.

questions.q: What does the passage mainly describe?
options: A sledding competition in a town park
The dangers of heavy snow for families with cars
How a snow day helped the writer feel part of a new town
Why schools should close whenever it snows
questions.explanation: The text begins with a newcomer who knows nobody and ends with a classmate's nod and the feeling that the town had opened a door. The car and the sleds are details along the way.

questions.q: What can be inferred about the writer's old city?
options: It had a larger park than the new town
It had heavier snow than the new town
School was never closed there
Days off school there were caused by storms, not snow
questions.explanation: In the old city a day off school meant a storm, and people stayed indoors with the windows shut. The writer's surprise at "enjoy it" shows that snow days were something new.

questions.q: What did the family use to clear the snow from the front door?
options: A kitchen tray
Their gloves
A shovel from the car
A plastic sled
questions.explanation: Paragraph 2 says the door would not open until they had pushed the snow away with a kitchen tray. The sled belongs to a later paragraph, and the car could not even be found.

questions.q: In paragraph 5, "soaked through" is closest in meaning to
options: torn in several places
completely wet
too small to wear
frozen stiff
questions.explanation: Gloves that are soaked through are wet all the way to the inside, which is why the children finally went home.

questions.q: In paragraph 3, "it" in "stay safe and enjoy it" refers to
options: the school
the message
the day off
the bus
questions.explanation: The school is telling students to enjoy the day it has just cancelled. The next sentences confirm this by comparing what a day off school meant in the old city.

questions.q: What does the writer mean by saying "the town had opened a door" in the last sentence?
options: The school had reopened after the snow day
Tomas had invited the writer to his house
The roads were finally open again after the snow
The writer had started to feel accepted in the new town
questions.explanation: The sentence follows Tomas's nod in the corridor, a sign of friendship from someone who had been a stranger. The door is a picture of being welcomed, not a real road or building.

questions.q: The writer had never seen snow before that morning.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The family was not ready for such heavy snow and the old city had storms rather than snow days, but the passage never states whether the writer had seen snow before.

passages.title: The Album Nobody Opened
passages.passage:
At the top of my grandmother's wardrobe, behind a box of winter blankets, there is a photo album with a dark green cover. I had known it was there for years, but nobody ever took it down. Last summer, when my grandmother broke her wrist and could not do much for herself, she asked me to bring it to her, and we spent three afternoons turning the pages together.

The first photographs were black and white and no bigger than a matchbox. In one, a serious young man in a white shirt stood in front of a wooden school with about thirty barefoot children. "Your grandfather," she said. "His first job. He was nineteen and terrified of them." I had only ever known my grandfather as a quiet old man who fed the chickens, and I found it hard to connect him with the stiff figure in the picture.

Further on, the pictures became larger and turned to colour, though the colours had faded to orange and pale blue. There was my mother at about my age, with a haircut she has since begged us never to mention, standing beside a bicycle that was clearly too big for her. There was a wedding in the rain, a house being built, and a whole page of a baby I did not recognise until my grandmother laughed and said it was me.

What struck me most was not the pictures themselves but how much my grandmother remembered around them: who had taken each photo, what had been said, what happened the next day. None of that was written anywhere. If she had not told me, it would have stayed inside her head.

Before I went home, I photographed every page with my phone and typed her stories underneath. My cousins now argue about which of them will keep the green album one day. My grandmother says that they are welcome to it, as long as they remember to open it.

questions.q: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Grandchildren should visit their grandparents more often when they are ill
A family cannot decide who should own a valuable album
Old photographs lose their colour if they are stored badly
Looking through a family album with a grandmother revealed stories that would otherwise be lost
questions.explanation: The writer's strongest point is that the memories around the photos were not written anywhere and would have stayed in the grandmother's head. The faded colours and the cousins' argument are smaller details.

questions.q: Why did the grandmother finally ask for the album?
options: Because the writer found it while looking for blankets
Because her grandchildren had been asking to see it
Because she had injured her wrist and could not do much else
Because she wanted to give it to one of her grandchildren
questions.explanation: Paragraph 1 links the request to the summer she broke her wrist and could not do much for herself. Giving the album away comes up only at the very end, and as a joke.

questions.q: How did the writer feel when looking at the photograph of the grandfather?
options: Proud that he had been a teacher
Surprised that the young man was the same person as the old man she knew
Sorry that the children in the photo had no shoes
Amused that he had been afraid of the children
questions.explanation: The writer found it hard to connect the quiet old man who fed chickens with the stiff young teacher. That gap between the two images is the feeling described.

questions.q: In paragraph 3, the word "faded" is closest in meaning to
options: lost their strength and brightness
been painted over
become brighter
changed into black and white
questions.explanation: Colours that have faded to orange and pale blue have grown weak with age. The photos were still in colour, just a dull version of it.

questions.q: In paragraph 4, "None of that" refers to
options: the names of the people in the pictures
the afternoons the writer spent with her grandmother
the photographs in the album
the grandmother's memories connected with each photo
questions.explanation: The previous sentence lists what the grandmother remembered: who took each photo, what was said, what happened next. None of that was written down, meaning those memories.

questions.q: Why does the writer include the grandmother's last remark?
options: To explain why the album was kept on top of the wardrobe
To show that she does not care who inherits the album
To make the point that an album only matters if it is actually looked at
To suggest that the cousins will argue for many years
questions.explanation: The condition as long as they remember to open it echoes the title and the first paragraph, where nobody ever took the album down. The value is in the looking, not the owning.

questions.q: The writer's mother does not like being reminded of her old haircut.
options: True
False
Not Given
questions.explanation: The mother has since begged us never to mention the haircut, which is exactly this idea in other words.
